paras: The New Orleans race riot of July 1900 was a series of white mob attacks on Black residents of New Orleans, Louisiana, after a Black man, Robert Charles, killed two police officers on July 24. Over four days mobs killed several Black people and burned the Thomy Lafon school for Black children. Esther Fields, a washerwoman beaten in her doorway, was among the wounded named in wire casualty lists, and a grand jury later indicted alleged mob leaders.

According to the Rev. D. A. Graham, writing in the Indianapolis Freeman, Charles resisted arrest on Dryades Street on July 23 and early the next day shot Captain John T. Day and Patrolman Lamb at his lodging. Crowds at the scene "proposed vengeance on the property and on the Negroes in the hovels around" until police dispersed them, and wire reports also cited white workers' resentment of Black labor on the levee.

On Wednesday, July 25, mobs of whites attacked Black people throughout the city and chased them from the streets. A Wilmington, Delaware, dispatch described "a mob of white boys" that hunted Black people until 3:30 a.m., dragging Alex Ruffin from a streetcar and stabbing T. P. Anders. A dozen or more of its members found Esther Fields standing in her door and beat her, leaving "several gashes on head." Others shot George Morris, Dan White and Baptiste Filo, aged 75; August Thomas was killed on Custom House Street, and Lewis Taylor died of wounds received at the French Market. Six or seven whites were hit by the mob's own fire.

Attacks continued on July 26, when Mayor Capdevielle swore in special police and Governor Heard ordered out 1,500 militia. About 1 a.m. on July 27 a mob that "claimed to be seeking a couple of notorious negroes" broke into the Rousseau Street home of Hannah Mabry, 62, and shot her dead. Later that day Charles was shot dead after a siege on Saratoga Street; a man found in the house was shot by the crowd while in police hands, and another was killed on Gallatin Street. That night a mob burned the Lafon school, claiming arms were stored there.

With 1,500 special police and the militia on the streets and bars closed, order returned by July 28. Harry Mabry identified two arrested men, George Flanagan and Mike Foley, as members of the mob that killed his mother; one account said police had encouraged the rioters. On August 15 a grand jury indicted five more white men, including Ernest F. Carl for the school fire, S. F. McCowan as the alleged "main leader and organizer" of the July 25 mob, and Joseph Wagner for Thomas's murder. A week later it indicted William Burke, a militiaman, for the killing in the police wagon; no report of a trial was found.
A mass meeting of Black residents urged people not to sell their homes and leave, and Black ministers condemned Charles and thanked the mayor for protection.

White papers ran wire copy from August 1, often under headlines putting Charles first, such as the Fairfield News and Herald's "NEGRO MURDERERS. Inflames the Mob." The same dispatches called the rioters "hoodlums" and boys, and the Cameron County Press headlined that militia had been called out "to Protect Negroes from the Assaults of Murderous Hoodlums."

Black weeklies were harsher. The Plaindealer saw "the spirit of the Klu-Klux, without the rags of disguise," and the Colored American, likening the rioters to China's Boxers, rejected the excuse that they were "mere boys." The Indianapolis Freeman wrote that Black people were "shot while fleeing, shot while standing, shot when in hiding," and the Cleveland Gazette faulted federal officials' silence.

Black editors divided over Charles: the Freeman called him a murderer who should have faced a court, while the Plaindealer and Seattle Republican praised his resistance. Esther Fields appeared by name only in white casualty lists; the Plaindealer told of "a poor Negro girl" beaten in her door.

Death counts varied: one in a July 27 dispatch, three in the Wilmington account, one dead and seven fatally wounded in another list. The man killed in custody was first called Burke Jackson, but on August 4 Jackson was reported arrested alive in Mississippi.

reader.title: New Orleans race riot (1900)
bases: White mobs hunted Black residents across the city over several days, beating, shooting and killing people on streets, streetcars and in homes and burning a Black school (A10, A17, A5, A1).

Independent wire accounts and casualty lists (A10, A17, A12, A5) agree on the mob attacks, the named victims including Esther Fields, and the school burning, and Black papers (A18, A27, A30) confirm the attacks.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Mobs of white boys and hoodlums, inflamed by Charles's killing of officers and by labor resentment, hunted Black people for hours while police were helpless; the better class deplored it.

accounts.label: Casualty-list digest
accounts.gist: Lists one dead, seven fatally wounded and five injured Black people, including Esther Fields, and seven whites accidentally wounded; says police sympathized with and encouraged the mobs.

accounts.label: Grand jury
accounts.gist: Indicted white men as leaders of the July 25 mob, the school burning and the killing of Thomas, and a militiaman for the custody killing.

accounts.label: Black editorialists
accounts.gist: A Klan-like mob of 'American Boxers' killed innocent Black people while 'responsible' whites let it run; the 'boys' excuse was rejected.

accounts.label: Black New Orleans meetings
accounts.gist: A mass meeting urged residents not to flee and expressed confidence in the authorities; ministers condemned Charles and thanked the mayor.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'NEGRO MURDERERS. Inflames the Mob' put Charles first while the text called the mob lawless.
'Militia Is Called Out to Protect Negroes from the Assaults of Murderous Hoodlums'; the Marshall County text called the mob 'a howling mob of fiends'.
The Kansas City Star blamed men in authority who justify mobs.
A Nebraska paper blamed Democrats for the 'race war'.
'The spirit of the Klu-Klux'; rioters as 'American Boxers'; 'shot while fleeing, shot while standing'.
Courts not mobs; Charles a murderer but the mob 'out for blood'.
The Savannah Tribune and Indianapolis Recorder ran wire copy that blamed Charles for 'all the trouble' and praised the citizens' police.

info: Mob attacks on Black residents began July 24-25, 1900, peaked Wednesday night July 25 to 3:30 a.m. July 26 (Esther Fields beaten that night), continued July 26-27 (Mabry killed about 1 a.m. July 27; Lafon school burned night of July 27); order restored by July 28

Across New Orleans: St. Charles Ave. and Howard St., Henry Clay Ave. streetcar, Jackson Ave., Poydras Market, Rampart St., French Market, Custom House and Villere streets, Gallatin St., Rousseau St., Lafayette Square, Thomy Lafon school at Sixth and Rampart

Black victims named: killed or died—August Thomas, Lewis (Louis) Taylor, Baptiste Filean/Filo/Gileal (listed as killed in one list, fatally wounded in others), Hannah/Anna Mabry, an unknown man on Gallatin St., an unknown man shot in police custody; wounded—Esther Fields (washerwoman), Alex Ruffin, T. P. Anders, George Morris, Dan White, James Nelson, Thomas Sanders, Charles Washington, Nathan Brown, Lewis Edwards, William Armstrong

No accusation against the victims; the mobs were described as avenging the killing of police officers by Robert Charles; the Mabry mob claimed to seek 'notorious negroes'; the school mob claimed arms were stored there

White mobs described as boys and 'hoodlums'; later named: George Flanagan and Mike Foley (identified in the Mabry killing), Ernest F. Carl, S. F. McCowan of Kenner, Joseph Wagner, militiaman William Burke
